h: Free, fascinating and right by the marina
p: Entry to the National Waterfront Museum is free, like the other national museums of Wales, so it is a brilliant option for families watching the pennies. You can drop in for an hour, head off for lunch and wander back later without worrying about getting your money's worth.

The building is part of the appeal. It combines a historic listed dockside warehouse with a striking modern slate and glass extension, a neat way of joining old Swansea with new. The galleries cover everything from coal and copper to transport, energy and the inventions that came out of Wales, and there are plenty of hands-on displays for curious fingers.

Swansea was once known as Copperopolis, thanks to the huge copper industry that grew up along the river, and the museum helps you understand how that shaped the city and the people who lived there. It is a great backdrop for kids doing school projects, and adults often find it more moving than they expected.

Allow around two hours to explore properly. Afterwards, the marina is right outside for a stroll among the boats, and the Dylan Thomas Centre is close by if you want to learn about the city's most famous writer. Swansea Market in the city centre is great for Welsh cakes and local produce.
If you have more time, follow the sweep of Swansea Bay round to Mumbles for ice cream, the pier and seaside views, or carry on to explore the stunning beaches of the Gower peninsula.
